advances: Quantitatively realizes every finite lattice table that extends to a globally log-concave function by the actual fiber-volume tables of common convex bodies, with arbitrarily small multiplicative error in the normalized curvature-cutoff score. The realization preserves the ambient integer dimension, including when the positive support has smaller affine rank. Consequently, the same uniform scalar inequality holds for all actual profiles if and only if it holds for all globally extendable finite profiles. This is a reduction of the scalar selection problem, not a proof of the required uniform lower bound.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The actual-body midpoint inequality is used through accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`; the remaining realization, convex-roof, lattice-normalization, approximation, and limiting arguments are proved above.
proof:
For a globally extendable table, applying its extension inequality to \(j+v,j-v\) gives \(w_j^2\ge w_{j+v}w_{j-v}\), and a positive pair has a positive midpoint. Thus the curvature is finite and nonnegative on \(\mathcal U_j\). Also \(0\in\mathcal U_j\), \(\alpha(0)=w_j\), and \(\Delta_j(0)=0\). The same properties for actual profiles are part of accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`. For any of these finite tables, replacing a cutoff by the largest curvature value not exceeding it leaves its cutoff sum unchanged and decreases its denominator. Hence the maximum defining \(K\) is attained among finitely many centers and curvature values. Multiplying every weight by a positive scalar multiplies \(\alpha\), \(B_j^\Delta\), \(K\), and \(W\) by that scalar and leaves \(\Delta_j\) unchanged.

For the first assertion, the function \(1-V/d\) is continuous, concave, and bounded below by \(1-B/d>1/2\). Convexity of each inequality \(y_i\le1-V(x)/d\), together with \(y_i\ge0\) and convexity of \(P\), proves convexity of \(C_d\). It is closed and bounded, hence compact. It contains the nonempty open set \(\operatorname{int}P\times(0,1-B/d)^d\), so it is full-dimensional. Its fiber over every \(x\in P\), including every boundary point, is exactly the closed cube \([0,1-V(x)/d]^d\). Fibers outside \(P\) are empty. This proves the asserted actual volume formula and the exact positive integer support.

The global functions equal to \(e^{-V}\), respectively \((1-V/d)^d\), on \(P\) and zero outside \(P\) are log-concave. For the second one, use concavity and positivity of \(1-V/d\), followed by monotonicity and concavity of the logarithm. For the first, use convexity of \(V\). If an endpoint is outside \(P\), the defining log-concavity inequality has zero right-hand side. Thus all relevant curvatures are nonnegative.

For \(0\le t\le1/2\), one has \(-t-t^2\le\log(1-t)\le-t\). The upper bound follows because the derivative of \(\log(1-t)+t\) is \(-t/(1-t)\le0\); the lower follows because the derivative of \(\log(1-t)+t+t^2\) is \(t(1-2t)/(1-t)\ge0\), and both expressions vanish at zero. Apply these inequalities with \(t=V(z)/d\) and multiply by \(d\). Since \(V(z)^2/d\le B^2/d\), exponentiation proves \(e^{-\varepsilon}w_z\le w_z^{(d)}\le w_z\). Off the common support, both sides are zero. Summation proves the total-weight bounds, and taking minima proves the \(\alpha\) bounds.

On the support, put \(e_z:=\log(w_z^{(d)}/w_z)\in[-\varepsilon,0]\). The exact curvature difference is \(2e_j-e_{j+v}-e_{j-v}\), which belongs to \([-2\varepsilon,2\varepsilon]\). Consequently, at the same center \(j\), for every \(L\ge0\),
\[
B_j^{\Delta^{(d)}}(L+2\varepsilon;w^{(d)})\ge e^{-\varepsilon}B_j^\Delta(L;w),
\qquad
B_j^{\Delta^{(d)}}(L;w^{(d)})\le B_j^\Delta(L+2\varepsilon;w).
\]
In this display, the arguments after the semicolon only specify the table used in the already defined cutoff sum. These inclusions count both orientations and the zero displacement. Dividing by the respective denominators and using \(1+L+2\varepsilon\le(1+2\varepsilon)(1+L)\) proves both bounds for \(K\). Combining them with the total-weight bounds proves the normalized comparison. As \(d\to\infty\), both multiplicative comparison factors tend to one. When \(B=0\), \(V=0\), so exact equality of the tables is immediate.

We now prove the roof assertions for a globally extendable table. Finite log-concavity gives, for every convex combination of sites in \(A\),
\[
f\left(\sum_{z\in A}\lambda_z z\right)/M
\ge\exp\left(-\sum_{z\in A}\lambda_z h_z\right)>0.
\]
This follows by induction from the two-point inequality, omitting zero coefficients. Therefore every lattice point of \(P\) has positive table weight, so \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=A\). For fixed \(x\in P\), the feasible coefficient set in the roof definition is a nonempty closed subset of the finite probability simplex. It is compact, so the minimum is attained. Every feasible objective lies in \([0,B]\). Combining minimizing coefficient vectors for two points proves convexity of \(V\).

At \(z\in A\), the preceding log-concavity inequality shows that every feasible coefficient vector has objective at least \(h_z\), while the coefficient vector concentrated at \(z\) has objective exactly \(h_z\). Hence \(V(z)=h_z\) at every lattice site in \(P\), including its boundary.

For completeness, continuity holds on the whole polytope, not only its relative interior. Work in any real affine coordinates on \(\operatorname{aff}P\). The epigraph of the roof is exactly the set of \((x,t)\) for which there exist coefficients \(\lambda\ge0\) satisfying \(\sum\lambda=1\), \(\sum\lambda z=x\), and \(t\ge\sum\lambda h_z\). Eliminating the finitely many coefficient variables yields finitely many linear inequalities in \((x,t)\). Indeed, replace equalities by pairs of inequalities and eliminate one variable at a time: existence of that variable is equivalent to every lower bound being at most every upper bound, together with the inequalities independent of it; if one class of bounds is empty, the other class imposes no additional restriction. This is a finite exact elimination procedure. Every resulting inequality can be written as \(a_i\cdot x+b_i t\le c_i\). Since the epigraph contains \((x,t)\) for arbitrarily large \(t\) at every \(x\in P\), each \(b_i\le0\). The inequalities with \(b_i=0\) only constrain the domain. Those with \(b_i<0\) give finitely many affine lower bounds on \(t\), and there is at least one such bound because \(V\ge0\). For \(x\in P\), the roof is their maximum. It is therefore continuous relative to all of \(P\).

If \(P\) is full-dimensional, apply the first assertion to this roof and the normalized table \(w/M\). Multiplying the first vertical coordinate of the resulting body by \(M\) multiplies every \(d\)-dimensional fiber volume by \(M\) and preserves compactness, convexity, and full dimensionality. This gives the second assertion in full rank and all its scalar comparisons by the scaling observation.

Here is the complete construction in smaller rank. Assume first that \(1\le r:=\dim\operatorname{aff}A<n\). Fix \(z_0\in A\), let \(E:=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}(A-z_0)\), and let \(\Gamma:=E\cap\mathbb Z^n\). The group \(\Gamma\) is saturated: if \(k v\in\Gamma\), with \(v\in\mathbb Z^n\) and nonzero integer \(k\), then \(v\in E\), hence \(v\in\Gamma\). It contains the differences \(A-z_0\), which span \(E\).

Choose a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) of \(\Gamma\). To justify this basis choice, every subgroup of \(\mathbb Z^n\) has a basis by induction on \(n\): its first-coordinate image is either zero, when one works in \(\mathbb Z^{n-1}\), or \(k\mathbb Z\) for some \(k>0\); choose an element with first coordinate \(k\), subtract its unique required integer multiple from each element, and apply induction to the kernel in the remaining coordinates. The resulting integer-independent vectors are real-linearly independent because a real dependence between integer vectors implies a rational dependence by rational row reduction. Thus their number is the real dimension of their span, which here is exactly \(r\).

Set \(Uu:=\sum_{i=1}^r u_i g_i\) and \(\phi(u):=z_0+Uu\). This is an affine bijection from \(\mathbb R^r\) onto \(\operatorname{aff}A\), with \(\phi(\mathbb Z^r)=\operatorname{aff}(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n=z_0+\Gamma\). This uses the complete intersection lattice, not the possibly smaller group generated by selected support differences. Put \(P^\sharp:=\phi^{-1}(P)\), \(V^\sharp:=V\circ\phi\), and \(w_u^\sharp:=w_{\phi(u)}\) for \(u\in\mathbb Z^r\). The domain \(P^\sharp\) is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^r\). Its lattice support is exactly \(\phi^{-1}(A)\), and the roof properties and global log-concavity survive the affine pullback.

There is also an exact scalar normalization. If \(j=\phi(j^\sharp)\in A\), every ambient displacement \(v\) with \(j\pm v\in A\) lies in \(E\cap\mathbb Z^n=\Gamma\), so uniquely \(v=Uu\) for \(u\in\mathbb Z^r\). Conversely every positive reflected intrinsic pair maps to such an ambient pair. Its endpoint weights, \(\alpha\), and \(\Delta\) are unchanged. This bijection preserves both orientations and zero, so all cutoff sums, \(K\), and \(W\) are identical in the two descriptions. In particular, there is no lattice-index or determinant multiplier; the vertical coordinates and their volume measure have not been changed.

Apply the first assertion in integer dimension \(r\) to \(P^\sharp,V^\sharp\), producing a body \(\widehat C_d\subset\mathbb R^{r+d}\) with normalized fiber volumes \((1-h_z/d)^d\) at \(z=\phi(u)\in A\). We next restore integer dimension \(n\) while preserving these exact volumes. Choose a linear map \(Q:\mathbb R^{n-r}\to\mathbb R^n\) whose image is a complement of \(E\). Compactness of \(P\), discreteness of \(\mathbb Z^n\), and \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=A\) imply \(\rho:=\operatorname{dist}(P,\mathbb Z^n\setminus A)>0\).
Indeed, a sequence of lattice points with distances to \(P\) tending to zero would be bounded, hence would have a constant subsequence whose value belongs to \(P\), a contradiction. Choose \(\delta>0\) so small that \(\|Qt\|<\rho\) whenever \(t\in[-\delta,\delta]^{n-r}\). Then \(\bigl(P+Q[-\delta,\delta]^{n-r}\bigr)\cap\mathbb Z^n=A\). Containment of \(A\) is immediate. Any other lattice point in that sum would have distance less than \(\rho\) from \(P\), contradicting its definition.

Take the affine image of \(\widehat C_d\times[-\delta,\delta]^{n-r}\) under \((u,y,t)\mapsto(\phi(u)+Qt,y)\). The map is an affine isomorphism of the ambient real spaces, so its image is a convex body in \(\mathbb R^{n+d}\). At an integer base \(z\in A\), directness of the complementary sum forces \(t=0\) and \(u=\phi^{-1}(z)\), so the vertical fiber is exactly the corresponding fiber of \(\widehat C_d\). No other integer base lies in its projection. Finally multiply the first vertical coordinate by \(M\). This proves precisely the formula for \(\widetilde w^{(d)}\) in the original integer dimension. Any original zero-volume boundary fiber has weight zero; whether the new zero-weight fiber is empty or lower-dimensional has no effect on the table or on any scalar comparison.

If \(r=0\), then \(A=\{z_0\}\), \(M=w_{z_0}\), and \(B=0\). For any \(0<\delta<1/2\), the body \((z_0+[-\delta,\delta]^n)\times[0,1]^d\), with its first vertical coordinate multiplied by \(M\), has the exact table \(w\). This handles rank zero without invoking a statement in integer dimension zero.

It remains to verify that all actual profiles belong to the globally extendable class and to prove the equivalence. Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^{n+d}\) be an arbitrary convex body and define \(g(x):=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_x)\) at every real base \(x\), including zero-volume fibers. This is finite and nonnegative, and its positive integer support is finite because the projection of \(C\) is compact. We prove its global log-concavity using only the accepted midpoint inequality and elementary limiting arguments.

If \(g(x),g(x')>0\) and \(x\ne x'\), form the auxiliary body
\[
D:=\{(s,y)\in[0,2]\times\mathbb R^d:
(x+(s/2)(x'-x),y)\in C\}.
\]
It is compact and convex. It is full-dimensional in \(\mathbb R^{1+d}\): take \(d+1\) affinely independent points in its positive-volume fiber at \(s=0\) and one point in the fiber at \(s=2\). Their affine span has dimension \(d+1\). Its midpoint fiber is positive since it contains the half-size translate of either positive endpoint fiber toward any point in the other. Applying the curvature nonnegativity in accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14` to this actual body in integer dimension one, at center \(j=1\) and displacement \(v=1\), gives \(g((x+x')/2)^2\ge g(x)g(x')\). The same inequality is immediate if \(x=x'\) or one endpoint value is zero. Thus it holds at all real pairs, not only at integer bases.

The function \(g\) is upper semicontinuous, including at zero-volume boundary fibers. To see this, all vertical fibers lie in one compact box. If \(x_k\to x\) and \(C_x\ne\varnothing\), then for every \(\eta>0\), one has \(C_{x_k}\subset C_x+\eta\overline B_d\) for all sufficiently large \(k\), where \(\overline B_d\) is the Euclidean unit ball. Otherwise compactness supplies points in a subsequence of the fibers converging to a point of \(C_x\) while staying at distance greater than \(\eta\), a contradiction. Hence \(\limsup_k g(x_k)\le\operatorname{vol}_d(C_x+\eta\overline B_d)\). As \(\eta\downarrow0\), these compact neighborhoods decrease to \(C_x\), and continuity of finite volume from above gives \(\limsup_k g(x_k)\le g(x)\). If \(C_x\) is empty, then \(x\) is outside the closed projection of \(C\), so the nearby fibers are eventually empty as well.

Repeated midpoint interpolation gives the log-concavity inequality for every dyadic coefficient. For positive endpoint values, approximate any \(t\in(0,1)\) by dyadic coefficients and use upper semicontinuity at the interpolated base; the lower bounds converge to \(g(x)^{1-t}g(x')^t\). If either endpoint value is zero, the desired inequality is immediate. Therefore \(g\) is a globally log-concave extension of the actual lattice table. This argument explicitly allows positive support of smaller affine rank and all zero-volume fibers.

Assertion (ii) consequently implies (i). Conversely, assume (i) and take any table in (ii). The bodies \(\widetilde C_d\) constructed above have the same integer dimension \(n\) and positive total volume. Thus \(K(\widetilde w^{(d)})/\widetilde W^{(d)}\ge a\,2^{-n}\) for every sufficiently large integer \(d\). The quantitative normalized comparison proves convergence to \(K(w)/W\), giving (ii) with exactly the same constant. A strict violation transfers by the same convergence. For a sequence, choose the continuous dimension separately for each table so that \(e^{\varepsilon}(1+2\varepsilon)\to1\); then the upper comparison preserves \(2^nK(w)/W\to0\). No inference that a positive uniform constant exists has been made.

Finally, the distinction from weaker lattice conditions is concrete. In \(\mathbb Z^2\), put weight one at \((0,0),(1,2),(2,1)\), weight \(e^{-1}\) at \((1,1)\), and zero elsewhere. The four positive sites have distinct parities, so every same-parity positive pair consists of a repeated site; all integer-midpoint log-concavity inequalities hold. Every coordinate line has at most two consecutive positive sites, so its one-dimensional sequence is log-concave as well. Nevertheless, \((1,1)\) is the average of the three sites with weight one. A globally log-concave extension would have value at least one there, contradicting its prescribed value \(e^{-1}\). This verifies why neither weaker hypothesis suffices for the roof matching and realization assertions proved here.
statement:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer. For a nonzero, nonnegative, finitely supported table \(w=(w_z)_{z\in\mathbb Z^n}\), write \(A:=\{z:w_z>0\}\) and \(W:=\sum_z w_z\). Say that the table is globally extendable if there is a finite-valued function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty)\) with \(f(z)=w_z\) at every \(z\in\mathbb Z^n\) and
\[
f((1-t)x+ty)\ge f(x)^{1-t}f(y)^t
\quad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n,\ 0<t<1),
\]
where a zero endpoint makes the right-hand side zero. In particular, the extension agrees with the zeros of the table; arbitrary finite subsampling is not the hypothesis.

For each positive integer center \(j\in A\), use the scalar notation of accepted fact `280b299bc1e87c14`: \(\alpha(v):=\min\{w_{j+v},w_{j-v}\}\), \(\mathcal U_j:=\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:\alpha(v)>0\}\), \(\Delta_j(v):=\log(w_j^2/(w_{j+v}w_{j-v}))\) for \(v\in\mathcal U_j\), and \(B_j^\Delta(L):=\sum_{v\in\mathcal U_j:\Delta_j(v)\le L}\alpha(v)\) for \(L\ge0\). Displacements are oriented and include zero. Write
\[
K(w):=\max_{j\in A,\ L\ge0}\frac{B_j^\Delta(L)}{1+L}.
\]
Thus \(K(w)\) is exactly the maximized scalar expression in that accepted fact, and its \(W\) remains the total weight, not the table. The same definitions apply to the actual table \(w_z=\operatorname{vol}_d(C_z)\), with zero assigned to empty or lower-dimensional fibers. All tables in the assertions below have nonnegative curvature on their positive reflected pairs.

First, let \(P\subset\mathbb R^n\) be a full-dimensional compact convex polytope with \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\ne\varnothing\), and let \(V:P\to[0,B]\) be continuous and convex, where \(B\ge0\). Set \(w_z=e^{-V(z)}\) on \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\) and zero elsewhere. For every integer \(d>2B\), the single set
\[
C_d:=\{(x,y)\in P\times\mathbb R^d:0\le y_i\le1-V(x)/d\text{ for }1\le i\le d\}
\]
is a convex body in \(\mathbb R^{n+d}\). Its actual table is \(w_z^{(d)}=(1-V(z)/d)^d\) on \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n\), and zero elsewhere. With \(\varepsilon:=B^2/d\), the supports agree exactly, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
e^{-\varepsilon}w_z&\le w_z^{(d)}\le w_z &&(z\in\mathbb Z^n),\\
e^{-\varepsilon}W&\le W^{(d)}\le W,\\
e^{-\varepsilon}\alpha(v)&\le\alpha^{(d)}(v)\le\alpha(v)
&& (j\in A,\ v\in\mathcal U_j),\\
|\Delta_j^{(d)}(v)-\Delta_j(v)|&\le2\varepsilon
&& (j\in A,\ v\in\mathcal U_j),\\
\frac{e^{-\varepsilon}}{1+2\varepsilon}K(w)&\le K(w^{(d)})\le(1+2\varepsilon)K(w),\\
\frac{e^{-\varepsilon}}{1+2\varepsilon}\frac{K(w)}W
&\le\frac{K(w^{(d)})}{W^{(d)}}
\le e^{\varepsilon}(1+2\varepsilon)\frac{K(w)}W.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here superscripts denote the same scalar definitions for the indicated table. In particular, the normalized score converges to \(K(w)/W\) as \(d\to\infty\). If \(B=0\), the tables agree exactly for every positive integer \(d\).

Second, let \(w\) be any globally extendable finite table in \(\mathbb Z^n\), with \(n\ge1\). Put \(M:=\max_z w_z>0\), \(h_z:=-\log(w_z/M)\) for \(z\in A\), \(B:=\max_{z\in A}h_z\), and \(P:=\operatorname{conv}A\). Then \(P\cap\mathbb Z^n=A\), and the convex roof
\[
V(x):=\min\left\{\sum_{z\in A}\lambda_z h_z:
\lambda_z\ge0,\quad\sum_{z\in A}\lambda_z=1,\quad
\sum_{z\in A}\lambda_z z=x\right\}\qquad(x\in P)
\]
is attained, convex, continuous relative to \(P\), takes values in \([0,B]\), and satisfies \(V(z)=h_z\) at every \(z\in P\cap\mathbb Z^n\).

For every integer \(d>2B\), there is a full-dimensional compact convex body \(\widetilde C_d\subset\mathbb R^{n+d}\) whose actual table is precisely
\[
\widetilde w_z^{(d)}=
\begin{cases}
M(1-h_z/d)^d,&z\in A,\\
0,&z\notin A.
\end{cases}
\]
All preceding scalar comparisons hold for \(w\) and \(\widetilde w^{(d)}\) with the same \(\varepsilon=B^2/d\). If the affine rank of \(A\) is \(r<n\), the construction first uses the primitive affine lattice \(\operatorname{aff}(A)\cap\mathbb Z^n\), then takes a sufficiently thin transverse product. There is no change of ambient integer dimension or lattice-index factor. Rank zero is included and has an exact realization for every \(d\ge1\).

Finally, for every fixed \(a>0\), the following two assertions are equivalent:

(i) For every \(n,d\ge1\) and every convex body \(C\subset\mathbb R^{n+d}\) with positive total integer fiber volume, its actual table satisfies \(K(w)\ge a\,2^{-n}W\).

(ii) For every \(n\ge1\) and every globally extendable finite table in \(\mathbb Z^n\), one has \(K(w)\ge a\,2^{-n}W\).

A strict violation of the scalar inequality in (ii) transfers to an actual common convex body in the same integer dimension and some finite continuous dimension. A sequence with \(2^nK(w)/W\to0\) transfers as well. The global-extension hypothesis cannot be replaced here by coordinatewise log-concavity or by the inequalities at integer midpoints alone.
